title: Why Is Mongolia Trapped Between Just Two Countries?

minor: Shot 4 says goods sent 'by land or sea' must cross Russian or Chinese ground, but the later line 'unless it flies' admits the air route. Consider 'by land' only, or add 'almost anything'.
'most of Mongolia's petrol and diesel arriving by rail from Russia': the listed source supports the Russian origin, not the rail mode. Add a source or drop 'by rail'.
'carrying gas ... straight across Mongolia' sits awkwardly next to 'the exact route has not been made public'. Consider 'across Mongolia' without 'straight'.
'the largest single land empire in history': Taagepera supports 'largest contiguous land empire'. Use that wording or add a source.
'Tuva, also once ruled by the Qing' has no listed source. Add one, e.g. Britannica, Tuva.
'Mongolia is a member of the International Criminal Court' has no listed source. Add the ICC states-parties list.
'Weeks later' for the foreign minister's statement (December 2016) is fine, but the listed source is only 'November and December 2016'.
The 1279 figure is a Taagepera estimate and could be attributed aloud ('by one estimate').
'postponed talks' after the Dalai Lama visit implies a link. It is Reuters-reported, but could be attributed ('China said it postponed talks').

shots.vo: So why does Mongolia only border Russia and China, and is it trapped?
The answer starts at Kyakhta, in 1727.
shots.title: *Kyakhta*, 1727

shots.vo: Picture a high, wide plateau in the middle of Asia, about 2,400 kilometres from west to east.
That makes Mongolia bigger than France, Germany, Britain and Italy put together, and the second-largest landlocked country after Kazakhstan.
Yet only about 3.5 million people live here, roughly two per square kilometre, the emptiest country in the world.
Almost half of them live in a single city, Ulaanbaatar, often called the coldest national capital on Earth.
The border with Russia runs about 3,452 kilometres along the north and north-west, through forest, mountains and open steppe.
The border with China is longer still, about 4,630 kilometres, running along the south, east and west.
Together that is 8,082 kilometres of border, and not one kilometre of it touches a third country.

Just beyond these peaks lies Kazakhstan, but a thin strip of Russian and Chinese land keeps the two apart.

shots.vo: One main railway runs south from Ulaanbaatar to Erenhot, and much of the trade moves along it or by truck.
At Erenhot, on the Chinese side, passenger carriages are lifted onto new wheels before the journey goes on.
That is because Mongolia's rails, like Russia's, sit 1,520 millimetres apart, while China's sit 1,435.
And who buys? In 2023, about nine in every ten dollars of Mongolia's exports went to China.
Coal leads the list: that year Mongolia sold a record 69.6 million tonnes of it abroad.

shots.vo: In 1206 a steppe leader named Temüjin took the title Genghis Khan and united the Mongol tribes.
Under his heirs, around 1279, their empire covered about 24 million square kilometres, the largest single land empire in history.

stat.label: Mongol Empire at its height, about 1279 (Taagepera, 1997)

shots.prompt: Horsemen as small silhouettes crossing a vast plain toward far mountains, top third dark and plain sky, duotone archival plate in dark slate and one muted orange, no faces, no text

shots.vo: But it soon split into rival khanates, each ruled by a different branch of Genghis Khan's family.
In 1368 the Mongol rulers of China were pushed out, and their realm shrank back to the steppe where it began.
Then the Manchu Qing dynasty rose in the east and drew the Mongols in, the southern groups first, from 1636.
In 1691, at Dolon Nor, the Khalkha, the main northern Mongol group, swore loyalty to the Qing emperor.
Meanwhile Russia was pushing east across Siberia, and in 1689 it signed its first border treaty with the Qing at Nerchinsk.
In 1727, at Kyakhta, the two empires drew the line between Siberia and Mongolia.
For over a century, traders met at Kyakhta to swap Russian furs for Chinese tea, carried across the Mongol steppe.
So Mongolia sat inside the Qing empire, fenced by Russia to the north. Then, in 1911, revolution broke out against the Qing.
On 29 December 1911, the northern Mongols enthroned a Buddhist leader, the Bogd Khan, as ruler of an independent state.

headline.text: Bogd Khan enthroned in Urga as Mongolia breaks from the Qing

shots.prompt: Map of Qing-era Asia with Outer Mongolia shaded as a newly independent state, Inner Mongolia and China left in another colour, muted painted style, blank labels.

shots.vo: In February 1912 the last Qing emperor gave up the throne. Inner Mongolia's southern Mongols stayed under the new Chinese republic.
Then came a crowded decade: limited self-rule in 1915, Chinese troops back in 1919, and revolution in 1921.
In July 1921, Mongolian revolutionaries and Soviet Red Army units took the capital, then called Urga, today's Ulaanbaatar.
In 1924 the Mongolian People's Republic was declared, the world's second communist state, closely tied to Moscow.
To the north-west, Tuva, also once ruled by the Qing, was absorbed into the Soviet Union in 1944.
But the Chinese government still claimed Mongolia as its own. Would it ever accept the new state on its map?
Beijing argued the new republic inherited all Qing lands, citing Article 3 of the 1912 Provisional Constitution, which listed Mongolia as Chinese territory.
At Yalta in February 1945, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill secretly agreed that Mongolia's status quo would be preserved.

map.label: Yalta, 1945: 'The status quo in Outer-Mongolia shall be preserved'

shots.vo: That October Mongolia's authorities ran a plebiscite, a vote of the whole people, with a Chinese observer present.
The official count, reported by the Chinese government, was 487,409 votes for independence and none against.

shots.vo: In January 1946 the Republic of China recognised Mongolia's independence, and the southern edge became a line between states.
The exact line was fixed by a treaty with the People's Republic of China, signed on 26 December 1962.
That line now divides the Mongols: about 6.3 million live in China, against about 3.5 million in Mongolia.
When Moscow and Beijing fell out in the 1960s, Mongolia sided with Moscow, and Soviet troops were based on its soil.
The last of those troops left in 1992. Mongolia could now choose its friends, but never its neighbours.
So who wants what here today? Start in the south, with China, the buyer of most of what Mongolia digs.
Oyu Tolgoi, one of the world's largest copper and gold mines, lies about 80 kilometres north of the Chinese border.
The mining group Rio Tinto owns 66 per cent of it, and Mongolia's government holds the other 34.
Nearby, coal from the Tavan Tolgoi field runs south on a railway opened in 2022 to the crossing at Gashuunsukhait.
In 2014 Beijing and Ulaanbaatar raised their ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership, which China calls mutually beneficial.
In November 2016 the Dalai Lama visited Ulaanbaatar; China, which calls him a separatist, postponed talks with Mongolia.

shots.vo: Now the north. Russia sells Mongolia most of its fuel, and owns half of its main railway company.
In September 2024 Russia's President Vladimir Putin made an official visit to Ulaanbaatar.
Mongolia is a member of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, which had issued a warrant for his arrest in 2023.
In October 2024 the court's judges found Mongolia had failed to arrest him, and sent the matter to its member states.

Mongolia says it courts "third neighbours" to widen its options, including the United States, Japan, South Korea, the EU and India.
The phrase is usually traced to a 1990 visit by US Secretary of State James Baker; it became policy in 1994.

shots.vo: In 2019 Washington and Ulaanbaatar declared a strategic third neighbour partnership, yet the two capitals are more than 10,000 kilometres apart.
Friends far away still cannot change one fact: every train, truck and pipe must cross Russian or Chinese ground. So what could?
First, a pipeline. Russia's Gazprom plans Power of Siberia 2, carrying gas from western Siberia to China straight across Mongolia.
Gazprom says it would carry up to 50 billion cubic metres of gas a year.

shots.vo: If it is built, Mongolia could earn transit fees, but its two neighbours would also be bound together across its land.
Second, more rails south, carrying coal straight into China and, supporters say, easing the long truck queues.
That could bring more income, but also an even bigger share of trade going to one buyer. Safety or risk?
Third, reach farther. In 2016 China, Russia and Mongolia signed an economic corridor plan for trade and transport links.
And in May 2023 Emmanuel Macron became the first French president to visit Mongolia, with uranium and critical minerals on the table.
Yet anything those partners buy must still leave by Russian or Chinese rail, road or pipe, unless it flies.
Each road would change what crosses Mongolia's borders. None of them would, on current plans, change where those borders are.
So Mongolia is not simply trapped between two giants: it balances them, and with no third door that balance looks hard to change.
Next, a strip of land drawn so two empires would never touch: Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor, between Tajikistan and Pakistan.
